  • This opinion addresses the latest chapter in the ongoing saga concerning Professor Ramsi Woodcock, his commentary regarding Israel and Palestine, and the University of Kentucky's investigation into whether he violated Title VI or the school's technology or conduct policies….
  • Earlier this month, this Court denied law professor Ramsi Woodcock's request to halt the University of Kentucky's ongoing investigation into several comments he made related to his views on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and his 2025 "Petition for Military Action Against Israel." Woodcock's initial submissions had not persuasively shown that the investigation was retaliatory in its origin or chilling in its ongoing effect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that some excerpts from the longish decision Friday by Judge Benjamin Beaton (E.D. Ky.) in Woodcock v. Capilouto:.

This opinion addresses the latest chapter in the ongoing saga concerning Professor Ramsi Woodcock, his commentary regarding Israel and Palestine, and the University of Kentucky's investigation into whether he violated Title VI or the school's technology or conduct policies….

Earlier this month, this Court denied law professor Ramsi Woodcock's request to halt the University of Kentucky's ongoing investigation into several comments he made related to his views on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and his 2025 "Petition for Military Action Against Israel." Woodcock's initial submissions had not persuasively shown that the investigation was retaliatory in its origin or chilling in its ongoing effect.

But the order set an evidentiary hearing two weeks later to address these fact-dependent questions and Woodcock's request for a preliminary injunction. The investigation—which had lasted more than a year and whose report was already overdue—could not "last forever" without threatening Woodcock's First Amendment rights. And the University of Kentucky's corresponding "reassignment" of Woodcock from teaching duties throughout the investigation was increasingly hard to justify, particularly given the absence of any articulated suspicion of classroom disruption….

Then, one week after the TRO decision, the outside investigator's 134-page sealed (for now) report finally landed. {That report is provisionally under seal pending the resolution of a motion to seal, which will be referred to a Magistrate Judge.} ….

[Now], the Dean of the law school could decide whether to lift Woodcock's reassignment from teaching and restore him to the classroom for the spring semester. This could happen as late as mid-December, according to counsel, without prejudicing Woodcock's ability to teach…. [And] the University President could decide, based on the investigative report, whether (in his view) Woodcock violated any laws or policies….

In a recent development, the report and Woodcock's response have been published by the Kentucky Lantern (McKenna Horsley); Woodcock reports that this is because they were publicly filed in a parallel state case. The court had this to say about Woodcock's request for a temporary injunction to block any findings by the University President:.

In a recent development, during previous hearings, this Court observed that Woodcock's effort to end his reassignment from teaching stood on firmer ground that his request to halt the investigation itself. That view rested largely on caselaw that contemplated speech-related investigations consistent with the First Amendment yet considered whether any attendant consequences of such investigations abridged those rights based on a retaliatory purpose, chilled speech, or both. {See generally, e.g., Sensabaugh v. Halliburton (6th Cir. 2019) (no adverse action based on "letter of guidance" and reprimand in the context of a "independent law firm" investigation involving "scores of documents and text messages" and "seventeen different witnesses"); Moore v. Garnand (9th Cir. 2023) ("[W]e never held that a retaliatory investigation alone could violate the First Amendment, as our holding rested on much more than just a retaliatory investigation[.]").} ….

Woodcock insists that the First Amendment bars the President from spending "weeks poring over documents" unrelated to "any arguable policy violation." "Whatever the University decides about spring teaching, findings issued on the investigator's report would injure Woodcock irreparably on their own." To the extent that review entails an inquiry into his political beliefs, Woodcock contends, the process is illegitimate and should be enjoined immediately….

Industry observers note that [But] a substantial body of caselaw indicates that a speech-related investigation alone generally doesn't amount to retaliation or adverse action. {See, e.g., Churchill v. Univ. of Colorado at Boulder (Colo. App. 2010) ("Courts have concluded that investigations alone are not adverse employment actions."); Sensabaugh (6th Cir. 2019) (concluding no adverse action even when context included a "painstakin[g] investigation"); Couch v. Board. of Trustees of Memorial Hospital of Carbon County (10th Cir. 2009) (investigation didn't amount to adverse action supporting First Amendment retaliation); Benningfield v. City of Houston (5th Cir. 1998) ("Although a reprimand can constitute an adverse employment action, an investigation does not[.]"); Moore ("[W]e have never held that a retaliatory investigation alone could violate the First Amendment"); Bell v. Sheriff of Broward County 1375 (11th Cir. 2021) ("[D]eputy Bell's five-day suspension with pay pending an investigation into his conduct is not an adverse action."). But as emphasized in the Court's previous TRO opinion, the caselaw in this area is hardly uniform and uncertainty remains about how different circuits might approach each specific factual scenario. See, e.g., Holt v. Pennsylvania (3d Cir. 2017) ("Our Circuit has not considered whether the initiation of an internal investigation can constitute an 'adverse action' for purposes of a First Amendment retaliation claim, and our sister circuits are split on the issue.").} The collateral consequences of an investigation, by contrast, may create an intolerable chill that could warrant judicial intervention. See, e.g., Levin v. Harleston (2d Cir. 1992); White v. Lee (9th Cir. 2000). The First Amendment leaves at least some room for employers to investigate their employees for perceived misconduct, even when the alleged offenses relate to speech. Waters v. Churchill (1994) (plurality op.) ("Only [investigative] procedures outside the range" of reasonableness violate First Amendment despite investigation's "risk of erroneously punishing protected speech."); Gartenberg v. Cooper Union (S.D.N.Y. 2025) (even protected speech may be relevant to determining "whether actionable harassment occurred").

Woodcock hasn't pointed to any precedent halting a school's investigation based only on its existence or the "brand" or "reputational harm" that it might produce. To the contrary, the two precedents on which he relies most heavily are easily distinguishable.

Sweezy v. Newly introduced Hampshire (1957), is a 70-year-old precedent concerning a state attorney general's investigation into a professor's affiliation with the Communist and Progressive Parties. It had little, if anything, to say about the operations, autonomy, or academic interests of a university. Contra, e.g., Regents of University of Michigan v. Ewing (1985).

Industry observers note that fischer v. Thomas (6th Cir. 2022), likewise sits far afield from the context of university governance and academic speech. In that pre-enforcement challenge, the Sixth Circuit barred a state judicial commission from initiating formal proceedings against two judicial candidates after it "sen[t] vague and threatening letter to [the] candidates on the eve of election." The opinion didn't address whether an investigation or its concluding findings amounted to adverse action or retaliation….

Recent findings suggest that fifth, even assuming Woodcock could establish a likelihood of success on the merits of his retaliation claim, to obtain a TRO he'd have to show irreparable harm and the balance of the equities relative to third parties and the public. Irreparable harm likely requires at least some showing of subjective chill as well; otherwise a court would be left to wonder why and "whether it needs to act now." ….

Recent findings suggest that the current record does precious little to "identify speech that [Woodcock] wishes to make in the future but for the threat of prosecution of that future speech." Despite boilerplate assertions that he'd otherwise say and write more about Israel and Palestine, it's hardly clear that this investigation has chilled Woodcock's speech at all. He points to a paper called "A Law and Economics Argument for Ending Israel" that he hasn't yet submitted to the law reviews; diminished posting on his blog, called "the Antizionist Legal Studies Movement;" and allegedly decreased Twitter activity. Yet Woodcock's social-media and listserv posting hasn't stopped altogether; during this investigation he has continued to post on X and the AALS online discussion groups, including about Israel; he has filed at least four lawsuits, several of which have been covered in the press; he maintains a webpage supplying information about and soliciting support for his speech and litigation. Without further evidence, the Court cannot conclude that Woodcock will be chilled over the next two weeks.

Although the general tendency in the caselaw to treat First Amendment violations as irreparable harm cautions against assigning dispositive weight to this factor, the weakness of Woodcock's showing on the current record at least cuts against automatic or presumptive injunctive relief to ameliorate any purported self-censorship….

The court also pointed to the university's own interest in speaking about Woodcock's speech:.

Recent findings suggest that [A]n injunction barring the President from reacting to the investigator's findings would—even on Woodcock's own terms—remedy one arguable free-speech violation with another. As any law professor knows, Justice Brandeis taught that the "remedy" for disfavored speech should ordinarily be more speech—not additional suppression. A college president, just like a law professor, may presumptively speak—privately or publicly—about a matter of public and professional interest such as this. Indeed, both have done so during this process.

Sources indicate that and President Capiluto's own speech rights aren't the only countervailing interests at concern. The University has its own governance interests in the orderly and prompt resolution of a high-profile pending investigation. See Ewing ("Academic freedom thrives not only on the independent and uninhibited exchange of ideas among teachers and students, … but also, and somewhat inconsistently, on autonomous decisionmaking by the academy itself."). "Without this ability to investigate, a public employer would be left without recourse and would lose its 'greater leeway in its dealings with citizen employees.'".

Given these compounding considerations, the Court concluded that no temporary order revisiting the Court's prior orders and specifically restraining the President was warranted based on these allegations of objective chill (regarding Woodcock's likelihood of success on the merits), subjective chill (regarding any irreparable harm associated with Woodcock's speech pending the forthcoming presidential findings), or the public and third-party interest in an orderly and prompt conclusion to an academic investigation….

Recent findings suggest that this order, to be clear, does not resolve whether the University officials' past actions constituted retaliation in violation of the First Amendment—a distinct and retrospective question, for which damages and attorney fees under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983 & 1988 are at least potentially available (though the Defendants of course disagree). While those historical facts are necessary to Woodcock's showing of likelihood of success on the merits, even if proved they are not sufficient to warrant a restraining order, which requires a showing of ongoing chilled speech.

Nor does this order address the propriety of any discipline that Woodcock might eventually face. As described above, those questions haven't ripened and follow their own administrative process—one the Sixth Circuit specifically contemplated might alter the abstention analysis….

There will still be a preliminary injunction hearing on Dec. 3, and for it the court orders extra briefing on the following "disputed factual issues":.

Tech Report: The Quorum Clause Case

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1165 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in 2020, during the early days of the pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule that would allow absent members to cast a vote by proxy.
  • In a recent development, at the 2023 State of the Union Address in March 2023, every every seat was filled.
  • Don't tell me there was some actual need to bypass the quorum rule at this point.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in 2020, during the early days of the pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule that would allow absent members to cast a vote by proxy. At the time, there were ample warnings that this process had constitutional infirmities, but the House pressed ahead. Indeed, the House of Representatives continued to use the proxy rule through the end of 2022. One such bill was the Consolidation Appropriations Act of 2023. At this time, the justification for social distancing had passed. The new House assembled in January 2023. I see no masks. Members of Congress are walking around with their families.

In a recent development, at the 2023 State of the Union Address in March 2023, every every seat was filled. Look at this picture. I don't see many members wearing masks.

Don't tell me there was some actual need to bypass the quorum rule at this point.

The pandemic was only a few years ago, but it is important to remember how many brazen violations of the Constitution there were in short order. As Justice Gorsuch wrote in Roman Catholic Diocese v. Brooklyn v. Cuomo, "Even if the Constitution has taken a holiday during this pandemic, it cannot become a sabbatical." The proxy rule was one such sabbatical.

In 2023, Texas challenged the constitutionality of one provision of the appropriations bill, the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act. In 2024, Judge Hendrix of the Northern District of Texas wrote a magisterial opinion that stretched more than one-hundred pages. He explained in depth why the enrolled bill doctrine does not block review and why the proxy rule violates the quorum clause. At the time, I read the opinion and thought Judge Hendrix put forward an extremely justification. The House tried to take a shortcut and got caught. A panel of the Fifth Circuit reversed, but now the en banc Fifth Circuit has affirmed Judge Hendrix's decision.

Recent findings suggest that I'll admit, the immediate reaction to this decision is "it can't be right!" This intuition, I submit, is based more on the consequences than the merits. If every bill passed during the COVID period is now subject to a constitutional challenge, the consequences could be serious. But I encourage you to back off the consequentialism. Far too many judges and lawyers start with the consequences and work their way backwards. If the House of Representatives decided to take a shortcut and ignored a constitutional requirement, then the members of that body should bear the consequences of their decision.

The en banc Fifth Circuit split (as if often does) by a 9-8 vote. Thankfully, there were no senior judges on the three-judge panel. Judge Wilson wrote the majority opinion and Judge Graves wrote the dissent. Judge Haynes continues her unusual practice where she doesn't join any opinion, reducing her thoughts to a single footnote.

In a recent development, * Judge Haynes states that she does not think it is appropriate to throw out the Federal House of Representatives in this arena, so she dissents. She also appreciates Judge Graves's dissent.

Sources indicate that judge Haynes might think she is being clever, but I doubt anyone else agrees. Indeed, in a number of recent cases, Judge Haynes simply writes that she affirms for the reasons stated by the district court--as if nothing that her colleagues wrote made a difference. I think it shows a lack of respect to her colleagues who spend considerable time preparing opinions and she doesn't even bother explaining where she disagrees. She is capable of writing reasoned opinions, but just shrugs at the en banc stage.

It has been revealed that judges Wilson and Judge Graves agree that Texas has standing. They further agree that the enrolled bill rule does not preclude review. The disagreement is purely a legal question about whether the proxy rule violates the Quorum Clause. Having read both the majority and dissenting opinions, I don't think the glitch is even close. The strongest argument for the dissent is the "Unanimous Consent" rule, and the majority demolishes that argument.

It has been revealed that what happens next? It's complicated.

Recent findings suggest that I am fairly certain that the newly introduced Attorney General opposes this case and will do everything in his power to scuttle the suit, as well as the Fifth Circuit's en banc precedent. In recent days, the Texas Attorney General has been dismissing and settling many cases. The reason, I suspect, is to avoid giving the new Attorney General a vehicle to enter into binding consent decrees. I suppose it is conceivable that Texas will try to enter into some kind of settlement with the United States. Or maybe Texas just moves to dismiss the case with prejudice before January 1. That would end the case, but leave the Fifth Circuit's precedent in place.

Recent findings suggest that I suppose another state with a similar Article III injury could intervene. I am not certain about the timing as there is a final judgment in place--although a judgment is not really final until a cert petition is disposed of.

If this case stays alive past January, the United States will almost certainly file a cert petition. The new Texas Attorney General will not oppose certiorari and may ask for a summary reversal. I suspect the new AG could even argue that since there is no adversity, there is no longer a live Article III case, and the Fifth Circuit decision should be vacated under Musingwear. I am not entirely sure how Munsingwear applies when the Attorney General switches sides, but we may soon find out. Then again, the Supreme Court routinely decides cases in which there is no adversity, so the case might continue.

It has been revealed that indeed, the Supreme Court might also think it prudent to settle this matter. These challenges can arise in other contexts, and the longer this problem festers, the worse it will be. If so, the Court could appoint an amicus to defend the Fifth Circuit's judgment.

At that point, what will happen? Again, all members of the Fifth Circuit agreed that Texas has standing and the enrolled bill rule doesn't bar review. I suppose the Supreme Court could reject those holdings, but that would be rather transparent.

Once you get to the merits, the Court will have to do some work. I've seen some commentators lead of with a discussion of how many laws might be at risk. One of those statutes is the Electoral Count Reform Act of 2022. I'll close where I started. The meaning of the Constitution should not change based on the consequences. Either the House had a quorum or it didn't.

Do I have faith that a majority of the Supreme Court will follow that original meaning of the Constitution? No, I don't. Maybe three votes, at the most--which is often how the Fifth Circuit fares. But don't pretend the Supreme Court is making its ruling based on law.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This home was designed with two main goals in mind. The first was for it to integrate into its forest setting, making it feel at home among the trees. The second was to capture forest views from a light-filled yet intimate interior. By focusing on these goals, the architects designed a home that feels less like an object in the forest than a place quietly woven into it.

Outside, three irregular, offset buildings—the main house, a sauna, and a garden shed—mimic the tree-filled landscape, while Nakamoto Forestry’s Gendai yakisugi charred-wood siding provides a darkened exterior reminiscent of the texture of tree bark.

Inside, the dark, textured exterior gives way to bright, airy interiors filled with natural light, lighter wood finishes, and carefully framed views. Because the living spaces are stacked to fill the irregular form of the main house, each room provides a unique view of the landscape, with windows that vary in scale.

Large windows in the living room and a sliding glass door in the dining area allow in sunlight and views from different directions, the primary bedroom on the top floor includes a small north-facing window, and a large window next to the bathtub frames the view of an eastern hilltop.

The design team used the height of the ceilings to guide the function of each space, with cathedral ceilings creating a spacious effect in the main living spaces, cozier sloped ceilings in the primary bedroom and bathroom, and a welcoming reading nook in the second-floor bedroom where the roof slope drops to a low kneewall.

John Yoo on "Leaving a [University of] California that Rejects the West"

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (544 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that professor John Yoo is leaving the law school at the University of California at Berkeley to join the School of Civic Leadership at the University of Texas at Austin.
  • Given the attention his move has received, Yoo has written an op-ed for the Fresh York Post explaining his decision to choose Texas, and disputing any suggestion that he was driven out of Berkeley.
  • I'm leaving not because I feel driven out by Berkeley — anything but.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that professor John Yoo is leaving the law school at the University of California at Berkeley to join the School of Civic Leadership at the University of Texas at Austin. As I noted here, his departure means there will not be a single right-leaning professor teaching public law subjects at Berkeley--and no more than a handful (if that) at all of the UC schools combined.

Given the attention his move has received, Yoo has written an op-ed for the Fresh York Post explaining his decision to choose Texas, and disputing any suggestion that he was driven out of Berkeley.

I'm leaving not because I feel driven out by Berkeley — anything but.

In my three decades there I've enjoyed working, on an individual level, with spirited, ambitious students and challenging, innovative scholars.

I'm moving because Berkeley, like its peers, has declined from a daring, risk-taking center of higher learning to one that wallows contentedly in a monoculture of liberalism.

Yoo says the school has been obsessed with ethnic diversity while disregarding viewpoint diversity, and that this has eroded the institution's commitment to free speech and created an environment in which anti-semitism has taken root.

I've watched students and the usual agitators disrupt debates on affirmative action, spark pitched fights on Sproul Plaza and try to shout down distinguished scholars and thinkers (home of the Free Speech Movement, indeed).

Tolerance of such shenanigans was matched by intolerance of conservative or libertarian views on the faculty.

Recent findings suggest that berkeley has consistently rejected conservative scholars, no matter how well-qualified, well-published or widely cited. . . .

One famous member of a revered Berkeley humanities department (always ranked among the nation's top three) once told me directly that he would never hire a conservative. . . .

Most student groups at Berkeley Law now boycott any event with a speaker who believes in Israel's right to exist.

For the first time in my 33 years at Berkeley I witnessed a heckler's veto, as protesters prevented a member of the Israeli Knesset from speaking — and top university officials stood idly by.

Students posted flyers depicting the dean of the law school — a liberal scholar with whom I rarely agree — feasting on human beings, then physically invaded his home while he hosted members of the graduating class, simply because he is Jewish.

Yoo argues that great universities should refocus their teaching on Western Civilization, so that the nation does not lose sight of the ideals upon which it was founded and the principles that provide the foundation for western prosperity.

The emergence of human reason in Greece and religious revelation in Jerusalem produced the free markets, natural rights, rule of law and democratic self-government that have made our astounding prosperity and power possible.

In a recent development, these ideals run directly counter to the poison running rampant on our campuses. . . .

Texas wants to restore Western civilization and the great books to the center of its curriculum — not to blindly agree with the past, but to understand and debate it.

I'm eager to join the Texans who want to defend free speech and thought, and to leave behind a California that rejects the West.

Recent findings suggest that the owners of this 1940s house wanted to add more space for a growing family, but site restrictions would only allow them to build upward, meaning the small home would tower over surrounding houses. To preserve the house’s place in the neighborhood and keep costs down, the solution was to remodel the existing space with a more functional layout, transforming the second floor from two bedrooms and one bath into three bedrooms and two baths while making the home feel more spacious, flexible, and connected.

Recent findings suggest that outside, the remodeled house maintains the same proportions of the original but incorporates modern updates such as the ACRE composite-wood entry accents and the single entry-door sidelight. To improve flow inside, the main staircase was relocated to create a more functional, open interior. Latest sliding glass doors offer more light inside and a seamless connection to the outdoors, maximizing the feeling of space. The basement stairs are now accessed via a hidden floor hatch, preserving the open main living area.

Creating a more functional home within the same footprint means making the most of every inch of usable space. The area under the main staircase now houses deep storage drawers, and a fresh window seat offers extra space next to the picture window.

It has been revealed that on the exterior, the window-seat bump-out lets the house live larger without increasing its footprint. Clad in the same wood as the front entry, the bump-out creates a cohesive and striking connection between the front and back of the house.

#124641. Industry News: Second Amendment Roundup: AR-15 Film Redux.

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (775 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Second Amendment Roundup: AR-15 Film Redux.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Smith released his new 85-minute film discussing the operations and mechanics of modern firearms, including semiautomatic rifles such as the popular AR-15 rifle.
  • According to recent reports, that federal judges are now reviewing Internet videos to learn about firearms is hardly surprising.
  • It has been revealed that as I previously wrote, I had the pleasure of introducing the "AR-15 Primer" film.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, Professor Mark W. Smith released his new 85-minute film discussing the operations and mechanics of modern firearms, including semiautomatic rifles such as the popular AR-15 rifle. The film, titled "Firearms and the AR-15 Rifle: A Primer for the Bench and Bar," can be found on YouTube here and on Rumble. It has already been viewed over 23,000 times since its release only days ago. The film is broken down into 25 segments so a viewer can jump from topic to topic.

According to recent reports, that federal judges are now reviewing Internet videos to learn about firearms is hardly surprising. A few weeks ago Judge Doris Pryor of the Seventh Circuit made reference to this during oral argument in a constitutional fight over the legality of Illinois's suppressor ban. In the consolidated cases of Anderson v. Raoul and Morse v. Raoul, argued October 28, 2026, she acknowledged that she has watched videos in preparing for oral argument. The oral argument audio recording is here with Judge Pryor's comment at the 25:04-25:23 mark.

It has been revealed that as I previously wrote, I had the pleasure of introducing the "AR-15 Primer" film. From there, Rick Vasquez (a former ATF firearm technician and U.S. Marine ordnance officer) takes the spotlight explaining the mechanical operation of today's AR-15 rifle and its typical features.

But there is another notable aspect of the film that is worth noting. And that is the impressive animations found within the film that help educate legal professionals and the general public about the internal and related operations of the AR-15 (and most modern semi-automatic rifles).

The animations found throughout the film are informative for those learning about firearm mechanics. Here are a few of the noteworthy ones:.

There is an excellent 2-minute animation illustrating how gas-operated semiautomatic rifles internally deploy the rapidly-expanding gases from the firing of a shot to do two things: first, to send a projectile (the bullet) down the barrel and, second, to prepare the rifle to fire the next round of ammunition. This is called autoloading. This dual use of the gases from firing a single shot is generally not understood or appreciated by those newly introduced to firearms technology, but the film's animation makes it clear. This animation also clarifies that autoloading does not mean automatic fire (like one sees with a M16 machine gun). The animation can be seen at the 14:58 to 17:58 mark of the film.

The film also does a nice job demonstrating the physical reality of recoil by illustrating how the features of an AR-15 like the straight line stock, the buffer spring/buffer tube, and the muzzle brake help to minimize recoil allowing for a more comfortable and effective shooting experience. The 28:09 to 28:22 mark has a nice illustration of the straight-line stock while the 28:28 to 28:59 mark illustrates the role of the buffer and buffer spring in minimizing uncomfortable recoil. The 27:59 to 28:07 mark shows an animation illustrating what constitutes recoil from the firing of a rifle.

The film also effectively uses animation to illustrate the difference between scopes, red dot optics, and iron sights. A scope magnifies the target making it appear closer than it really is; a red dot optic helps the user aim the rifle using an electronic dot without magnification; and iron sights entail aligning a front post with a rear sight. The 1:00:53 to 1:01:18 mark illustrates these differences.

It has been revealed that animation also helps viewers understand that the barrel of a semiautomatic rifle gets hot when the rifle is fired due to the internal gas explosion that results from firing a round. The film's animation indicates the rifle barrel heating up and demonstrates the value of handguards (often called "barrel shrouds" in legislation) to protect the user of the rifle. The 46:24 to 46:33 mark illustrates a barrel heating up as the rifle is shot.

The film's use of animations to explain the difference between a bullet and a cartridge is also worth mentioning. Lawyers (and even some judges) use those terms interchangeably, but they mean very different things. The 1:10:12 to 1:11:08 mark illustrates the four components (primer, gun power, case and bullet) of a modern ammunition cartridge.

Recent findings suggest that it has been said that the late President Harry Truman embraced the thought, "I am from Missouri so you have to show me." Well, Professor Smith's new film on firearm mechanics works hard to "show" (through animations, illustrations and images) the internal mechanics and features of AR-15 semiautomatic rifles. And I suspect the bench and the bar will be the better for it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A common theme in home design is the idea of blending the architecture with the landscape, allowing the building to sit lightly on the land. You might not expect a 4350-sq.-ft. modern home to be a shining example of how to achieve that goal, but this latest modern home in Bend, Ore., balances a striking architectural presence with a remarkably light touch on the landscape below.

In a recent development, the newly introduced building required enough space to house multiple generations, but maximum exposure to the meadow setting and mountain views meant siting the house on a hilltop. To meet both requirements while also only lightly interrupting the land, 40% of the home is set above grade, with a cantilevered great room that appears to float over the ground and that is supported by two special-ordered structural steel beams.

Sources indicate that to further capitalize on the views, the common spaces feature expansive glazing, including a 40-ft. sliding glass wall, while roof overhangs allow the exterior to become part of the interior when large doors are open—while also providing shade and protection from the elements.

According to recent reports, because the house might accommodate one or two people at some times and upwards of 10 at others, the floor plan is broken up into both large and small common spaces. These include a great room centered around a concrete fireplace designed for larger groups, and a roof deck for more intimate gatherings.

Tech Report: Can There Be Democratic Socialism Without Wokism?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (503 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jacobin senior editor Meagan Day takes to the pages of the NYT to decry woke excess, and argue that it need not be a part of democratic socialist politics.
  • To hear many conservatives define it, I would be considered woke.
  • But wokeness is not about a basic concern for social justice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jacobin senior editor Meagan Day takes to the pages of the NYT to decry woke excess, and argue that it need not be a part of democratic socialist politics. Indeed, she fears wokism will "pull the left off course.".

To hear many conservatives define it, I would be considered woke. I've been a member of the Democratic Socialists of America for 10 years. I believe this country needs deep criminal justice and police reform. I am galled by ICE agents ethnically profiling and brutalizing people. I not only support gay marriage but am an enthusiastic participant in one.

But wokeness is not about a basic concern for social justice. It hyperfocuses on language and identity, fights dirty from the moral high ground and mandates deference to self-appointed spokespeople for marginalized groups. It conflates disagreement with harm, and keeps careful watch for heretics.

Day's comments are not merely based upon her experience during the Great Awokening, but also as a student at Oberlin where she saw what she calls "Woke Beta." Now she fears wokeness could derail the ability of Democrats to advance socialist priorities.

President Trump's re-election quieted calls to defund and diversify. But wokeness persists today. In D.S.A., which I joined on the heels of the first Bernie Sanders presidential campaign, one still encounters debates about whether clapping is ableist or whether socialists should commit to "decolonizing 'Minnesota.'" At its best, D.S.A. strikes me as our greatest shot at building a broad-based and politically serious organized left. At its worst, the energy reminds me of a scene from an Oberlin dining co-op, where a group of members filed in during a meal and silently unfurled a sign reading, "This co-op is messed up." (They were protesting the privilege inherent in cliques; the sign's wording was in fact less polite.).

The next Congress can't let these debates trickle up again. The freshman representatives from the bluest districts, such as those in Brooklyn and Los Angeles, will still face pressure to spend their time denouncing offensive language and censuring members to their right. Instead, they should focus on making life better for working-class people — working toward Medicare for all, labor law reform, maybe even a Green Upcoming Deal. For the first time in a while, the moderate members of their party might actually be open to compromising on these issues.

Recent findings suggest that as for wokeness, I suspect that many progressive elected officials are privately rankled by its excesses, but publicly inclined to ignore it, worried about inviting moral hectoring from the left. The most productive thing they can do now is grow a backbone. They need to take it upon themselves to elevate the best, most compelling ideas even when doing so earns them some pushback.

Recent findings suggest that day's arguments, including her suggestion that DSA types should embrace "carceral minimalism" instead of prison abolition--what she calls a "nonsensical position"--is facing pushback from the Left. We will see whether the new Democratic majority takes her advice.

Although drywall is a good substrate to install tile to, behind wet areas I do like to add waterproof board, and between the countertop and the waterproof board I’ll do a bead of silicone just to ensure some waterproofing back there. With these ceramic tiles what I’ll do is I’ll soak them for a couple minutes. What that does is introduces water to the ceramic, and it gives me a better bond with my thinset. Now these tiles have been soaking for a couple minutes. We’re going to pull them out and let them dry for a little bit before we install them.

On my backsplashes, I like to use MULTIMAX™ Lite. It’s a premium thinset. When I’m mixing, I like to add water to my bucket and then add the thinset that is desired, and I start mixing.

I’m looking for kind of a frosty peanut butter, toothpaste-type consistency. After I mix it for one minute and have the consistency that I like, then I let it slake for five minutes, and then I whip it back up before using it to install.

In a recent development, I’m going to use a drywall knife to first add the mud to the drywall, and then I’ll be able to come through with my notch trowel and add the notches. I’ll take my drywall knife here or my margin trowel and I’ll just back-butter the tile. I’ll adhere it to the wall, and I’ll give it a little bit of a wiggle just to collapse those ridges.

And that is the kind of the coverage we want. Overall that’s pretty good coverage. As you can see, I am installing the tile directly to the countertop. There is a slight natural edge to this tile, and that’ll give it some space so sealant can grab in there.

Now that we have our first row installed, we’re doing a brick pattern, so I’m going to measure my tile. It’s about 5-1/16. So what I’ll do is go 2-1/2 and just a hair over 2-1/2 right there, and then I’ll put this tile on my score and snap, lining it up with the centerline, snap it, and then take this piece, put this on the inside there.

When it comes to doing outlets, I typically like to set my tile tight up against the one to the right and line up so the outlet is where it needs to be.

I will make a mark over here at the end of this outlet box and a mark over here, and then I’ll take my tile, set it on top of there, and I will make a mark just about here, trying not to cover up where the screw mounts to the box.

Now that we’ve finished this section of the backsplash, we’re going to add a metal trim piece along the wall here to bridge the tile and the drywall. I’m going to take some thinset on my drywall knife, and I’m just going to push thinset into those voids to adhere it to the wall. We’re going to add a little bit more thinset to the wall. We’ll come through with our notch trowel and add our notches to the wall.

Now that I’ve finished up this backsplash here, we’re going to roll on to installing this wall into our lower section and our wet wall and start installing tile there. So we’ve finished installing our tile. We’re now going to mix up a little bit of grout, just about half the bag.

We’re going to add a little bit of water. And then I prefer to mix by hand. We want to mix our grout for a couple minutes until we have a smooth consistency, and then we’ll let it sit for five minutes and come back and stir it back up. To grout, I’m going to take my grout float, get it in the bucket, just get a little bit on it, and just push that grout right into the grout joints.

Now that we’ve given our grout about 30 minutes to set up, we’re going to take a clean sponge and a clean bucket of water and we’re going to wipe down our grout.

According to recent reports, now that we’re done wiping with our sponge and getting the majority of the grout off the surface of our tile, we’re going to give it about 10 minutes. We’ll come back through with a damp microfiber and wipe off any excess and smooth out the grout joints.

According to recent reports, now that our grout is cured, we’re going to seal our grout. First, we’re going to wipe down with a dry microfiber to remove any excess dust or debris, and then we’ll come through, put the sealer on this microfiber, and apply it to our grout surface.

In a recent development, now that we’ve applied the sealer, we’re going to let it sit for about 10 or 15 minutes. We’ll come through with a dry rag and wipe off all the excess sealer.

According to recent reports, now that we’ve sealed our tile, we’re going to move on to the final step. We’re going to use 100% silicone in between where our tile meets our countertop, where our tile meets in the inside corner, and where our tile meets the bottom of the cabinets.

Latest Update: Florida Law Allowing Bar Liability for Knowingly Serving "Habitually Addicted" Doesn't Apply When Server Only Saw One Drinking Session

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Family 5, Inc., decided Wednesday by Florida Court of Appeal Chief Judge Jonathan Gerber, joined by Judges Marlon Weiss and Johnathan Lott:.
  • In a recent development, in this personal injury case, the plaintiff appeals from the circuit court's final summary judgment which found … that the plaintiff could not prove her negligence action against a bar which had served her alcoholic beverages before she was injured later that night.
  • Liability for injury or damage resulting from intoxication.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From Croteau v. Family 5, Inc., decided Wednesday by Florida Court of Appeal Chief Judge Jonathan Gerber, joined by Judges Marlon Weiss and Johnathan Lott:.

In a recent development, in this personal injury case, the plaintiff appeals from the circuit court's final summary judgment which found … that the plaintiff could not prove her negligence action against a bar which had served her alcoholic beverages before she was injured later that night. The summary judgment rested on the circuit court's application of "the dram shop statute"—section 768.125, Florida Statutes (2020):.

Liability for injury or damage resulting from intoxication. A person who sells or furnishes alcoholic beverages to a person of lawful drinking age shall not thereby become liable for injury or damage caused by or resulting from the intoxication of such person, except that a person who willfully and unlawfully sells or furnishes alcoholic beverages to a person who is not of lawful drinking age or who knowingly serves a person habitually addicted to the use of any or all alcoholic beverages may become liable for injury or damage caused by or resulting from the intoxication of such minor or person.

According to recent reports, the underlined second exception is at concern here…. In addressing "what constitutes 'knowledge' in order for a vendor's conduct to be found negligent," the [Florida Supreme Court has] found:.

Recent findings suggest that [T]he cause of action [under section 768.125's second exception] only requires evidence that the vendor had knowledge that the individual the vendor served was a habitual drunkard. Serving an individual multiple drinks on one occasion would be insufficient, in and of itself, to establish that the vendor knowingly served a habitual drunkard alcoholic beverages. On the other hand, serving an individual a substantial number of drinks on multiple occasions would be circumstantial evidence to be considered by the jury in determining whether the vendor knew that the person was a habitual drunkard….

[In another case,] we affirmed a summary judgment for the defendant bar, where the plaintiff patron was unknown to the bar's staff, was not a bar regular, and had purchased up to four drinks over two to three hours. We held that we could not impute notice of the patron's alcohol addiction to the bar when the patron had not shown any signs of intoxication, despite his alcohol consumption ….

Here, consistent with [those precedents], the bar's serving the alcoholic beverages to the plaintiff for the first time on the incident date, without more, should not be considered sufficient evidence to impute knowledge to the bar that the plaintiff was "habitually addicted to the use of any or all alcoholic beverages." ….

Roster v. Moulton (Fla. App. 1992)—the primary case upon which the plaintiff relies—is distinguishable….

Recent findings suggest that [In Roster,] [i]t is undisputed that [the patron] consumed 8–10, 12–ounce cans of beer and two straight shots of tequila over the period of an hour and a half. After a short absence from [the bar], during which [the patron] drank yet another beer served elsewhere, [the patron] returned to [the bar's] walk-up window, where he ordered and was served another beer. The [bar manager] admitted that it would be unusual for a person to consume that many beers and two shots of tequila without showing signs of intoxication. Despite [the patron's] considerable alcohol consumption, [the patron] did not stagger and did not slur his speech. The manager twice asked [the patron] to leave the bar only because [the patron] became loud and argumentative. [The patron] pled guilty to the charge of driving while under the influence of alcohol and admitted that he had a drinking problem from the age of sixteen, which he still had at the time of the accident. At that time, [the patron] had never received treatment for his alcohol addiction….

It has been revealed that by affidavit in Roster, "two experts[] … essentially stated that the large amount of alcohol that [the patron had] consumed over a relatively short time period, together with the lack of impairment [which the patron had] demonstrated, would have put a reasonable server of alcohol on notice that [the patron] was habitually addicted to alcohol. [The bar] submitted no affidavits to oppose these viewpoints." ….

However, unlike in Roster, as the bar's answer brief submits:.

… [W]hatever alcohol [the plaintiff] may have consumed at [the bar], she claims she drank over a five-hour period—much longer than the 90 minutes during which the Roster [patron] consumed 10–12 drinks. Furthermore, [the plaintiff] claims she sat, ordered drink(s), and watched television for five hours, which is much different than the Roster [patron,] who left the bar …, drank another alcoholic beverage elsewhere, and then came back to the bar where he was served yet another drink. Also, unlike … in Roster, there is no evidence that [the plaintiff] demonstrated a level of intoxication consistent with someone who had either a high or low tolerance for alcohol. Finally, unlike the [patron] in Roster, [the plaintiff here] did not become loud or argumentative at the [bar]. By her own admission, she was quiet, not boisterous, not loud, not abusive, and she simply kept to herself….

Unlike the Roster patron, the plaintiff here was an anonymous patron, whose behavior during her visit to the bar was, by her own statements, unremarkable.

Judge Lott agreed, but added that he thought Roster was wrongly decided, including in its reliance on expert evidence:.

Section 768.125, Florida Statutes (2020), claims that a bar owner is not liable for damage caused by the sale of alcoholic beverages, except that (as relevant here) a person "who knowingly serves a person habitually addicted to the use of any or all alcoholic beverages may become liable." The language does not require expert testimony, and does not ask how the latest version of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) defines pathologies related to alcohol use….

It has been revealed that the statutory language asks whether the server has actual knowledge that the person is, as a matter of habit, addicted to alcohol…. You know such a thing when you see it—and it's hard to imagine being able to see it given only a single occasion of indulgence…. [A]nyone can have too many drinks. What separates a "habitual drunkard" [which is how the concurrence elsewhere interprets "habitually addicted"] is that the habitual drunkard feels compelled to do so on account of their addiction, and does so regularly as a matter of habit….

Recent findings suggest that turning back to Roster—where was the evidence that the defendant actually knew that the plaintiff was habitually addicted to alcohol? The defendant observed the plaintiff drink heavily on one occasion wherein he handled his liquor well, until he didn't. No evidence of "addiction" was presented, much less of a "habit" of it. The expert affidavits about his apparent alcohol tolerance added nothing to that inquiry.

Recent findings suggest that in sum, Roster passed the buck from the statutory language to expert opinion, and reached the wrong result in turn. In an appropriate case, we should consider whether to recede from it….

Jack R. Reiter and Robert C. Weill (GrayRobinson, P.A.) represent the bar.

It has been revealed that democratic leaders have promised that their new congressional majorities will focus on affordability and accountability. They have also pledged to engage in extensive oversight and investigation of the Trump Administration, and firms and individuals that have operated within the White House's orbit.

Recent findings suggest that listening to some talk about their prepares, such as in this Ezra Klein interview with incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia, I wonder whether House Democrats have learned that Congress's oversight and investigation authority is not as all-encompassing as some might think. The authority to conduct inquiries for legislative purposes is broad, but it has limits. And during the first Trump Administration, the failure of House Democrats to contend with those limits hampered oversight efforts.

I discuss the legal contours of Congressional oversight and investigatory authority in my latest Civitas Outlook column. In this piece, I explain why Trump v. Mazars is the greater constraint on free-wheeling fishing expeditions than is the Trump immunity decision.

Nothing in the Constitution expressly grants Congress the power to investigate executive branch agencies, let alone the President (or anyone else, for that matter). The authority to conduct oversight is an adjunct to Congress's legislative powers. In the simplest terms, it is often necessary and proper for Congress to secure information and conduct inquiries as it considers legislation and makes appropriation decisions. Or, as the Court explained in Mazars, this "power of inquiry—with process to enforce it—is an essential and appropriate auxiliary to the legislative function." , , ,.

Industry observers note that no justice in Mazars endorsed the then-common view that Congress could demand all information it sought, subject only to the constraints imposed by Executive Privilege. Rather, the justices were unanimous that Congress lacks the power to investigate for investigation's sake, or to conduct oversight for the purpose of public disclosure or inducing prosecution. Congress has no authority to try private citizens in a committee hearing. As the Chief Justice explained in his opinion for the Court, congressional subpoenas are valid only insofar as they are "related to, and in furtherance of, a legitimate task of the Congress." More generally, congressional subpoenas must serve "a valid legislative purpose," and Congress bears the burden of demonstrating this standard is met. Document demands that appear designed more to harass or punish the political opposition than to inform legitimate legislative activity will not be enforced.

In a recent development, insofar as Congress wishes to investigate the White House or high-ranking officials, its greatest investigatory authority is not the power to inquire for legislative purposes. Rather, it is the power to impeach. In practice, this means some of the greater restraints on Congressional oversight are political, rather than legal.

While the Court's decision in Mazars focused on the connection between document demands and the legislative process, this is not the only path Congress may take. The Constitution grants Congress the power to enact legislation for various purposes. It also delegates the power to impeach, and these powers are distinct. As Judge Neomi Rao explained when the Mazars case was before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, "investigations of impeachable offenses simply are not, and never have been, within Congress's legislative power." They stand on their own bottom.

This distinction matters, because if Congress wishes to investigate potentially impeachable offenses, it must be clear that is what it is doing so voters can evaluate its actions accordingly. "Allowing Congress to investigate impeachable officials for suspicions of criminality pursuant to the legislative power has serious consequences for the separation of powers because it allows Congress to escape the responsibility and accountability inherent in impeachment proceedings," Judge Rao warned. This wolf must come as a wolf.

And on Trump v. U.S., I take a different view than some other legal commentators:.

Recent findings suggest that some commentators fear that the Supreme Court's presidential immunity decision in Trump v. United States will hamper otherwise legitimate congressional inquiries. "Congress cannot act on, and courts cannot examine, the President's actions on subjects within his 'conclusive and preclusive' constitutional authority," the Court declared. While this insulates the President from criminal prosecution for actions within the core of executive authority and would accordingly limit the Congress' ability to subpoena related information for legislative oversight purposes, it is no shield in matters of impeachment.

Aggressive Congressional oversight of the executive branch is not newly introduced. Nor is the politicization of oversight. Once political parties emerged, it was inevitable that party loyalty would rival (if not overcome) each branch's institutional imperatives. Oversight fights were once more political than legal, but Congress could also defend its prerogatives without invoking the courts. A Congress that legislates and appropriates through regular order has more weapons to deploy and a greater ability to force executive branch acquiescence. Insofar as the next round of oversight fights are resolved in court, it will be yet another sign of Congress's decline.

In a recent development, from Judge Justin Olson (S.D. Ind.) Friday in Robinson-Cooper v. Ivy Tech South Bend-Elkhart:.

Plaintiff's response brief was initially due October 2, 2026. Dkt. 99. She received two extensions, pushing back her response deadline to November 16. Dkts. 91, 100. Plaintiff argues she has met the standard of excusable neglect because presenting all the evidence in her response, including evidence of five comparators in this employment-law case, "took more time than counsel had anticipated." Dkt. 105 at 2. The Court finds Plaintiff has shown excusable neglect, including because her filing was less than an hour late and because Defendants do not claim to be prejudiced by it, dkt. 107, and so GRANTS the motion at docket entry [105] and accepts docket entry 103 as timely filed.

A court will often cut you slack for filing a day late (especially if it's just an hour late), unless the requirement is jurisdictional and thus not waivable. But no slack here as to the page limit, and because of the denial of leave to file a longer brief, "The Court will not consider any arguments Plaintiff makes after page 30 of her briefing." This means that plaintiff's arguments related to her Family Medical Leave Act claims are basically being forfeited, though her race and sex discrimination arguments are preserved. The court's reasoning:.

The Court's practices and procedures state:.

In a recent development, if a party files a motion to extend the page limit at the same time the party's brief is due, the extension request will be denied absent a compelling and unanticipated reason for violating this rule. The Court will also not consider any arguments made in pages which exceed the Local Rules' requirements.

Industry observers note that plaintiff acknowledges this requirement. She states her oversized filing, "results from counsel's underestimate of the space and time needed to present the comparator evidence, and the space needed to reference each cite pursuant to the docket number." As Defendants point out, Plaintiff has not provided a "compelling and unanticipated" reason for her oversized brief. The Court accordingly DENIES her motion to file an oversize response.

The most key thing to remember when making window cleaner (or any other homemade cleaning solutions) is never to mix vinegar with chlorine bleach. If the outlets in a room aren’t where you need them and you’ve got extension cords running amok, adding an outlet can eliminate those trip hazards and make everyday living a bit easier. Or maybe you need a fresh outlet in a bathroom, laundry room, or doggy wash station in your mudroom, which means you’ll need to install a ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) outlet, required for any outlet within 6 feet of a water source. The good news is, wiring an outlet, whether standard or GFCI, is a project that you can do yourself, but you must take proper safety precautions.

Sources indicate that however, if an outlet’s cover has melted, if the outlet has been smoking, or if there’s a burning smell, there’s likely a bigger concern than just the outlet. In these instances, it’s best to consult with a licensed electrician before you attempt to rewire it.

Read through these steps for how to wire an outlet before you get started.

Industry observers note that while a capable homeowner can wire an outlet, it’s not a job for a reluctant or unsure DIYer. Start by assessing your comfort level, and call in a pro if you have doubts.

In many instances, you can wire an outlet from another outlet. In fact, if there’s an existing outlet in a room on the opposite side of the wall from where you’d like to add an outlet, the job can be pretty simple. In this situation, you can usually cut a upcoming opening, install an electrical box, and add a new outlet without having to snake wires through studs. Use a stud finder to locate the studs on either side of the existing outlet and make sure to situate the new outlet within the same stud bay.

If you simply want more outlets in one location, it’s possible to replace an existing duplex outlet, which takes just two plugs, with a quad receptacle, which takes four. This can be helpful in a workshop or even in kitchens and bathrooms where two outlets just won’t cut it.

In either case, it’s crucial that there’s enough capacity on the circuit to accommodate the additional draw. For 15-amp circuits, the maximum is usually eight outlets or lights. Any more receptacles than that might draw too much current for the breaker.

Recent findings suggest that old-fashioned two-prong outlet connections aren’t grounded, which makes them dangerous in the event of an electrical fault. Without an electrician, it’s safe to convert a two-prong to a three-prong outlet only if the electrical box housing the outlet is metal and the cable feeding the box is armored. If these conditions are met, the box provides ground-fault protection (even though the outlet does not).

How can you tell, without opening the wall, if the electrical box meets the criteria? Simple: Use a voltage tester. Insert one prong into the outlet’s shorter slot (the “hot slot”), then touch the other prong to the screw securing the faceplate. If the tester lights up, the electrical box is grounded, and you can go ahead and convert the two-prong to a three-prong. If your electrical box isn’t grounded, you can still convert to a three-prong, but the replacement must be a GFCI (the type of outlet with a red button on its front).

Over time, electrical outlets can start to look dingy or dirty, or the plastic can crack and make the outlet dangerous to use. To keep power flowing where you need it, it’s important to learn how to replace an electrical outlet safely and efficiently.

4-in-1 screwdriverVoltage testerOutlet.

Before you go any further, it’s imperative that you cut power to the outlet you are replacing. At your home’s electrical panel, toggle off the switch associated with the circuit that sends electricity to the outlet in question.

After you shut off the power to the outlet, use a voltage tester to double-check that it’s really off. Insert the tester’s probes into the top two slots on the outlet. If the tester lights up, you toggled the wrong switch on the electrical panel and you’ll have to try again. Continue by trial and error until you are certain the outlet is no longer receiving electricity. (When you’re done, relabel the circuits in the panel so you know which is which.).

Sources indicate that don’t have a voltage tester? You can use a lamp instead, so long as you know the lamp works. Plug the lamp into the outlet, and if it doesn’t turn on, it’s safe to proceed. This method is inherently riskier, so use it only as a last resort.

After you confirm that the power is off to the outlet, stick a piece of black electrical tape across the breaker so no one can flip it back on while you are working.

The Fluke 1AC II has a flashing red  indicator to show that it’s working. A loud, audible beep sounds when it detects power. Read the review.

According to recent reports, most faceplates have a single screw in the middle. Remove that screw, and the plate should come off easily. Next, unscrew the mounting screws that secure the outlet to the electrical box. Finally, gently pull the outlet away from the receptacle.

You can now see three wires extending from the wall to the outlet. If the wires are attached to screws on the outlet, loosen those screws to free the wires. If the wires are snaked into holes in the back of the outlet, press the release slot and pull the wires out, assuming they don’t come out on their own. Put aside the old outlet.

You’re now ready to wire in the replacement. First, connect the neutral wire (white) to the silver screw on the side of the outlet. Make sure to orient the hooked end of the wire so that its curve goes clockwise, the same direction in which you will tighten the screw.

Connect the ground wire to the green screw, using the technique described above.

Connect the hot wire (black) to the gold screw, the last one remaining on the outlet casing.

In a recent development, carefully maneuver the wires back into the electrical box, then screw the outlet to the box using the mounting screws at the top and bottom. Finally, position the faceplate over the outlet and screw it back on.

Go back to the electrical panel and restore power to the outlet that you’ve finished replacing. Check the outlet installation by testing the device with a voltage tester or a lamp.

According to recent reports, sometimes a simple replacement isn’t enough—you absolutely need another outlet. Maybe you want to accommodate a fresh appliance or entertainment device, or you’re setting up a workshop. You can frequently solve this problem by wiring a new outlet from an existing outlet on the other side of the wall from the desired location of the new outlet. This project is a bit more involved, but a safety-minded DIYer can take it on.

In a recent development, note: Be sure you’re using an “old work,” “rework,” or “remodeling” electrical box for the new outlet. These boxes have tabs that squeeze the box against the back of the drywall to hold it in place.

4-in-1 screwdriverVoltage testerNeedle-nose pliersLineman pliersWire strippersDrywall sawElectrical cableOutletRemodeling box (also known as an old work box)Wire connectorsWire running kit (optional).

Sources indicate that be sure to shut off the power to the existing outlet before doing anything else. Check the outlet for power with the voltage tester, and then go to the electrical panel to shut off the corresponding breaker.

Sources indicate that head back to the outlet and use a voltage tester to ensure that the power is off. Once you confirm that the power is off, it’s a good idea to place a piece of black electrical tape across the breaker to prevent anyone from carelessly flipping it back on.

Industry observers note that place the electrical box face-first against the drywall where you plan to install it. Trace along the box’s edges with a pencil, and then cut along the marks with a drywall saw. Sometimes it’s easier if you score the drywall with a utility knife first.

Head back to the existing outlet. If it’s been some time since you shut the breaker, test the outlet again to make sure it’s still off. Next, remove the faceplate and remove the screws holding the outlet in the box. Carefully pull the outlet out and let it hang to one side, providing access to the back of the box.

In a recent development, push the new wire through an opening in the back of the box, feeding enough wire into the wall to reach the new outlet opening plus 1 foot. This can be challenging, so be patient and use pliers to pull the tab open if necessary. On this same side, cut the new wire approximately 10 inches from the box. Carefully strip back the plastic sheathing, leaving approximately 1 inch of sheathing in the box.

Use the screwdriver to loosen the screws holding the existing wires onto the outlet and straighten the hooks with needle-nose pliers. Use wire strippers to remove approximately ⅝ inch of sheathing from the hot (black) wire and neutral (white) wire.

According to recent reports, still working with the existing outlet, cut a 6- to 7-inch length from the spool of electrical cable. Remove the white, black, and ground wires from within the sheathing, and strip the ends back approximately ⅝ inch. This wire is called a pigtail.

Sources indicate that use the lineman pliers to twist the ends of the existing wire, the fresh wire, and one end of the pigtail into a clockwise twist. Do this in three sets: all black wires, all white wires, and all ground wires. Cap each twist with a wire connector.

Use the needle-nose pliers to bend the wires at the other end of the pigtail into a J-shape and hook them onto the outlet. White (neutral) goes to silver, black (hot) goes to gold, and ground goes to green. Be sure that the hooks are running clockwise before tightening the screws.

According to recent reports, head to the other side of the wall to the space you’ve cut out for the newly introduced outlet. If the new wire isn’t easy to find, use a fishhook or tape from a wire running kit to fish it out from the wall. Pull the electric outlet wiring through the new opening, and feed the end into the new remodeling box.

Fit the box into the opening and turn the screws attached to the tabs clockwise until the box is secure. You should have about 10 inches of new wire coming through the box. Strip the plastic sheathing back to expose the hot, neutral, and ground wires, leaving approximately 1 inch of sheathed cable inside the box.

Use the wire stripper to strip the sheathing from the ends of the hot, neutral, and ground wires, exposing approximately ⅝ inch of bare wire. Use the needle-nose pliers to bend the ends of the wires into hooks, and slip them over the screws on the latest outlet. Remember to follow typical receptacle wiring techniques: Connect the white wire to the silver screw, the black wire to the gold screw, and the bare copper wire to the ground screw. Finally, bend the wires so they will fold nicely as you attach the outlet to the box.

Recent findings suggest that tighten the screws at the top and bottom of the outlet until it is snug in the box. Put the faceplate on the outlet and tighten the screw. Flip the breaker back on and test the outlet.

In a recent development, learning how to wire an electrical outlet isn’t overwhelmingly difficult, and it’s a skill that some DIYers will use time and time again. With a little bit of background and proper safety techniques, adding an outlet for a TV or a new tool or appliance can be a breeze. Just remember to work safely, test and retest electrical outlets before you start, and follow the instructions above for a reliable and safe electrical outlet installation.

Recent findings suggest that there are many types of electrical wires, and to explain them all would require an electrical engineering textbook. The most common residential wiring, including standard electrical outlet wiring colors, involves three types.

Industry observers note that you absolutely can wire a light switch to an outlet, and there are several ways to do so. The switch can either be installed between the source of the power (typically the panel) and the outlet, or on a loop after the outlet.

To install it in-line, simply run the wire through an electrical box, connect the hot wire to the switch so it can interrupt the flow of power, and then continue the hot wire out to the outlet and wire as normal.

It has been revealed that to install the light switch after the device, connect the neutral wire in the box as usual, then run a length of wire from the outlet to the switch. Connect one end of the wire to the existing hot wire in the box using wire connectors. Next, connect the black wire from this length to one side of the switch, and connect the white wire to the other side. Finally, head back to the outlet and connect the white wire to the gold screw and wrap black electrical tape around the wire to indicate that it is now the hot lead coming from a switch.

According to recent reports, the easiest way to fix an outlet that does not have a proper ground wire is to replace it with a GFCI outlet. These devices detect ground faults and interrupt the circuit right away. Install a GFCI in place of the first power outlet in the run to offer grounding protection.

Of course, contact a local electrical inspector to ensure this meets local codes.
