In a recent development, during a power outage, a generator that runs on gasoline can provide enough juice to keep your lights on, your groceries from spoiling, and your fans spinning. Set up a portable unit outside your home, and connect appliances inside to its numerous outlets via extension cords. Exactly how many appliances it’ll power at once depends on the wattage that generator can handle.

While a portable generator might cost several hundred or even thousands of dollars depending on size and model, when compared to a standby generator, which would kick on automatically to power your home, it’s certainly less expensive. Plus, you may not need a professional electrician to install a portable generator, and you can easily take the unit with you should you move. All that mentioned, proper operation of the machine is crucial to ensure the safety of your family and your community.

Before you start up a portable generator, bear in mind these two essential considerations:.

Recent findings suggest that WEN’s 5600-watt generator has a push-button start and is powerful enough to run household essentials; noise level is about 88 dB. Read the review.

Because portable gas generators emit carbon monoxide while they’re running and for some time afterward, positioning the generator properly and practicing careful carbon monoxide safety is critical.

Before you start up the generator, check the fuel gauge and fill the tank with gasoline as needed. (Make sure the generator is on a level surface to get an accurate reading on the fuel gauge.) If you need to add fuel, consult the owner’s manual for fuel requirements.

Next, check the oil level, which is like checking the oil in your car. Locate the oil dipstick (often below a removable maintenance panel). Pull out the dipstick, wipe it off, and then re-insert it. Carefully pull the dipstick straight out once more, then look to see if the oil on the stick falls between the lower and upper limit marks imprinted on the dipstick. Add or change the oil if necessary, referring to your owner’s manual for how to add, what kind to use, and how frequently it needs to be changed.

Before plugging in, ensure that you won’t overload the generator by connecting more appliances and lights than it is rated to handle. Add up the starting and running wattage of the appliances you want to power simultaneously; refer to their respective user manuals or check the backs or sides of the machines to find this information. The total number should not exceed the wattage limitations of your generator. Check your user’s manual if you’re unsure of how many watts of power your generator can handle. Stagger the use of appliances if necessary to prevent overloading the generator.

It has been revealed that follow your user manual for instructions on turning on the machine. You typically will need to turn the circuit breaker off and turn the fuel valve on before starting it up. Give the machine a few minutes to warm up, then flip the circuit breaker on.

Industry observers note that use long, heavy-duty extension cords made for outdoor use to connect appliances to the generator one by one so as not to overload it. Examine cords before use to ensure they are in good condition with no rips or tears. The cord’s wattage rating should be greater than the wattage of what you’ve plugged into it.

To shut down the generator, turn off or disconnect the appliances plugged into it. Then refer to your user’s manual to power down the generator—typically you’ll need to turn the circuit breaker, engine switch, and fuel valve to the “off” position.

Wait until the generator is completely cooled down before storing it once power is restored. If you don’t anticipate needing it again for more than a month, drain the fuel and carburetor. Leaving old fuel can damage the generator’s internal parts. Refer to your owner’s manual for storage instructions.

In a recent development, when running a portable generator, safety is the name of the game. Keep these tips in mind before, during, and after use.

Maintaining healthy indoor air quality is essential for protecting members of your household from hidden carcinogens, allergens, and harmful particulates. Pollutants can enter your living space from a range of sources, including building materials that emit volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and poor ventilation that traps moisture and encourages mold growth.

While clues like window condensation, musty odors, or unexplained respiratory symptoms can signal trouble, invisible, odorless threats such as radon and carbon monoxide often go undetected without the right equipment. We spoke to indoor air quality experts to identify the top five indoor air pollutants in U.S. homes and how to fix or mitigate them.

This monitor impressed our product testers with accurate readings, and it connects to an app where users can find air quality reports for their home.

In a recent development, particulate matter—including tiny airborne particles like pollen, smoke, soot, and other debris—is one of the most common indoor air pollutants, notes Dr. Jaspreet Dhau, an expert on indoor air quality and purification and vice president of research and development at Molekule in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida. “Fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, which is a particle measuring 2.5 microns [micrometers] or smaller, is a concern because it can travel deep into the respiratory system,” says Dhau. Common sources include cooking, burning candles, using a fireplace, vacuuming, and even opening windows when outdoor pollution levels are high.

Industry observers note that VOCs are gases released by certain household products and materials such as paint, solvents, flooring, furniture, adhesives, cleaning supplies, air fresheners, and personal care products. “VOC levels may be higher during and after a home renovation, when upcoming furniture is brought into a home, or when products containing chemical ingredients are used without adequate ventilation,” says Dhau. For example, certain pressed wood furniture and building materials can release formaldehyde, he explains.

Industry observers note that carbon monoxide (CO) is a combustion byproduct, a pollutant released when something burns. “In a typical home, sources can include gas stoves, fireplaces, wood-burning stoves, furnaces, water heaters, candles, and tobacco products,” claims Dhau. “Carbon monoxide is especially dangerous because it’s colorless and odorless, making it difficult to detect without a working CO alarm.”.

Industry observers note that biological contaminants such as dust mites and pet dander are airborne pollutants that originate from living organisms, states Dhau. “Dust mites are a frequent problem and tend to collect in mattresses, carpets, upholstered furniture, and bedding. They can enter homes through open windows, pets, clothing, and HVAC systems,” he explains. Signs you might have a problem include frequent dust buildup on surfaces, allergy symptoms, excess pet hair and dander, and dust accumulating around air vents, adds Bill Myers, indoor air quality expert and group manager for technical sales at Panasonic Eco Systems North America.

Quiet, effective and easy to use, this commercial-grade unit cleans the air with a washable pre-filter, a carbon filter, and a HEPA filter.

Everyday activities such as cooking and showering introduce moisture into the home. “When excess moisture is not adequately removed, particularly in bathrooms, basements, and other low-ventilation areas, conditions can become more favorable for mold and mildew growth,” notes Meyers. You might notice foggy mirrors that take a long time to clear, condensation on windows, musty odors, bathrooms that remain damp long after use, and visible mold or mildew.

According to recent reports, power outages are top of mind now more than ever before—and for good reason. One in four households experience a power outage in a year, according to U.S. Census Bureau data, and 70 percent of those reporting outages were without power for 6 hours or more. These longer outages are not only disruptive; they can also be expensive, considering that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration recommends tossing perishable food kept in the refrigerator after just 4 hours without power.

Backup power promises comfort and security, which is why so many homes rely on a portable generator or power station. That category has grown from gas-powered generators to multi-fuel units, portable power stations, and whole-home batteries. The newest member of the family? A fridge backup.

Industry observers note that just in 2026, this latest style hard-debuted with models from three industry leaders: Bluetti’s Fridge Power, Jackery’s FridgeGuard, and Backup Core by BioLite. And the consumer response has been powerful. Bluetti’s Kickstarter hit 145 percent of its funding goal in 45 days. Jackery debuted as a Costco exclusive in June and expanded its retail distribution after hearing about customers carrying home multiple units. BioLite has released its Backup in two waves already, each selling out in weeks, and is taking orders now for January shipments. Clearly, homeowners want a backup built just for the fridge. Keep reading to learn more about what sets fridge backups apart and when one beats a generator.

According to recent reports, think of it like a larger version of the uninterruptible power supply (UPS) that you might use in a home office or with a high-end entertainment center to keep your connected electronics running during a brownout or blackout. A UPS in the home office might offer surge protection and enough battery life to run your computer for another 5 minutes so you can safely shut it down; this fridge-optimized backup can keep your most crucial kitchen appliance on for 15 hours or more.

And while we call them “fridge” backups, the design is actually much more versatile. Plug them in and slip the slim backups easily into any room to keep an vital appliance operational for hours: under a bed to power a CPAP machine, behind a bookshelf within cord’s reach of an air purifier, or behind the fish tank to maintain the family pet’s habitat.

Kickstarter backers for the Backup by BioLite—which first debuted in 2024 on the crowdfunding platform—“got it” immediately. “They understood the problem it was solving, and most questions revolved around understanding additional applications and setups beyond the fridge because the kitchen application was so intuitive,” notes Erica Rosen, the VP of Marketing at BioLite and Goal Zero brands. “For example, we got a lot of questions about sump pumps and if Backup could run one during an outage.” (Spoiler alert: It can.).

Today, homeowners (and renters!) have many options for backup power, each with its own set of pros and cons.

A standby generator or whole-home battery backup automatically kicks in to keep the essentials—if not the whole home—running during an outage. Each type of backup connects at the electrical panel with a transfer switch. As such, each is a larger investment (read: more expensive) and a permanent installation that requires a licensed electrician. These backups also require forethought about fuel. A standby generator will require a source of liquid propane and/or natural gas, whereas whole-home batteries are often charged from the grid before an event and potentially recharged via solar panels when the grid is down.

According to recent reports, A portable gas-powered generator is more affordable than a standby option, but should only be run outdoors, which creates some limitations. For starters, you need to be home to turn a portable generator on and connect to your appliance. Then, you’ll need a long, heavy-duty outdoor-rated extension cord to reach the kitchen. These generators operate loudly, emit exhaust fumes, and require you to store enough fuel to be ready for the worst. Assuming you have a good supply, though, you can keep your appliance(s) powered with minimal interruption using a reliable portable generator.

Recent findings suggest that A power station brings backup power indoors to power multiple electronics and small appliances. Power stations are the closest comparison. They are safe to use indoors or out and feature similar battery capacities. You can find options in the ballpark of 1 to 2 kWh for similar price points. They can, but may not always be, plugged in 100 percent of the time to act as a UPS. And importantly, they’re often too bulky to leave out next to a refrigerator 24/7.

In a recent development, A fridge backup offers instant power backup without a permanent installation. It’s ideal for the consumer who is looking for a user-friendly, set-and-forget setup and a safety net that offers enough power to keep a fridge running for approximately 15 hours while the power is out—longer if additional batteries are connected.

According to recent reports, “It’s [designed for] someone who wants peace of mind without having to think too much about backup power. Maybe you live somewhere with frequent storms, or you’ve come home after an outage to find everything in your freezer has spoiled,” says Beau Tyrrel, Product Manager at Jackery. “It’s also useful for renters and those who live in apartments and can’t install a whole-home backup system. All you need is a standard outlet, and you can take it with you when you move.”.

Industry observers note that the design is appealing in more ways than one, notes Luna Yan, affiliate marketing manager at Bluetti. A fridge backup solves spatial problems that come with more traditional portable power stations: “Traditional backup power systems are often bulky, making them difficult to accommodate in homes with limited space, particularly in kitchens and apartments.”.

Industry observers note that “When we set out to develop Backup, we knew the world didn’t need another box-format power station. We did a lot of user research and found that there was a meaningful gap between the power stations of the world and expensive whole-home backup solutions, and it was leaving a lot of people out of the resiliency conversation,” Rosen says. “As we explored ways to answer this, it became clear that form factor was going to be a really crucial element: If we wanted something plugged in permanently to enable automatic performance, it needed to be really easy and it could not take up precious living space.”.

In a recent development, it’s especially useful if you’re away when the power goes out and can’t move the fridge’s plug to a generator. Already plugged into the wall from setup, the backup’s stored power will be usable immediately. Each model’s mobile app demonstrates outage alerts, battery level, and power draw from anywhere.

“[A fridge backup is] also useful for renters and those who live in apartments and can’t install a whole-home backup system. All you need is a standard outlet, and you can take it with you when you move.”.

There’s a cost to every power outage. One of the biggest concerns for most homeowners is the spoiled food in a refrigerator after 4 hours without power. “Refrigerators are one of the few appliances in your home that needs to run around the clock,” Tyrrel claims. “When the power goes out, you could lose hundreds of dollars in groceries.”.

Sources indicate that A blackout can cost the average American household $117 in spoiled groceries, according to a survey of more than 1,000 Americans by the Texas electric provider Payless Power. One in five homes had it worse, losing more than $200 in groceries during a single outage.

In a recent development, using that average, we estimate that a $1,000 fridge backup pays for itself after 10 blackouts—potentially sooner in larger households or homes with especially packed fridges and freezers. For an area that experiences one to two extended blackouts in a year, this investment could earn its keep in as soon as 6 years—and these new backups are rated for 10 or more years of use.

Sources indicate that “Based on customer feedback, refrigerators are among the most crucial appliances to keep running during a power outage,” Yan claims. And for good reason: “Continuous refrigeration helps protect food, medications, and other temperature-sensitive items.”.

According to recent reports, if your utility manufacturer offers a Time-of-Use (TOU) electricity pricing proposal, any of these fridge backups can help you take advantage of the savings. TOU programs charge different supply rates based on when you use electricity, incentivizing customers to use more electricity when overall demand is low by charging less per kilowatt-hour (kWh) used. These “off-peak hours” vary by plan, but typically are overnight and early morning.

Recent findings suggest that for the average homeowner, the main way to save on these plans is to optimize the electricity usage you can schedule: when you charge an electric vehicle, run the dishwasher, and wash or dry a load of laundry. A fridge, of course, runs all day, and an efficient, Energy Star-certified model can use anywhere from 358 kWh for a compact top-freezer unit to 805 kWh per year for a large side-by-side refrigerator. You can’t optimize the always-on appliance without either a whole-home power bank that recharges in an off-peak hour for use during peak times or, now, a fridge backup. In a connected mobile app, customers specify the best times to charge (off-peak hours) and discharge (peak hours), effectively shifting the fridge’s grid use to cheaper hours.

According to recent reports, especially now, with rising concern about grid stability and the increasing frequency of natural disaster events that disrupt power, demand for energy backups is high. Each of these energy brands has sold out and replenished stock at least once already this year. So while you may be eager to set up your home with the first available fridge backup, here’s a comprehensive look at unit specs to help find the model best suited to your space and needs.

According to recent reports, bluetti’s fridge backup offers the largest base capacity—nearly double that of Jackery FridgeGuard, and expandable to 8 kWh (second only to BioLite’s 10.5 kWh). Divide the total cost by the capacity, and you’re paying about $470 per kWh, which is the most backup per dollar. One unit can power the typical modern fridge for 21 to 48 hours, and a maximized setup of FridgePower plus three BlueCell battery packs can power your fridge for 4 days. (Run time, of course, depends on the specific refrigerator’s energy consumption and usage conditions.) That makes the slim design even more impressive—though at 43 pounds, it’s a two-person job to wall-mount.

The mobile app provides battery levels, outage status, and charging progress, plus a place to choose among four UPS modes: Standard, PV Priority (which prioritizes solar power), TOU (Time-of-Use), and Custom. It even tracks local weather, alerts you when a storm approaches, and switches to fast charging if needed. An optional magnetic display (sold separately) provides at-a-glance information including percentage charged, energy output, and UPS modes—all without opening your phone.

Recent findings suggest that on paper, the Jackery fridge backup appears to be the unit most specialized for fridge use. It offers up to 15 hours of power in the slimmest profile. One outlet (for the fridge) and a single expansion option make it the least flexible of the three—but if the fridge is all you need, it’s a perfect fit. It’s effective, affordable, lasts up to 16 years, and takes only one person to install the lightweight unit on a wall mount (sold separately). It offers surge protection for your most important household appliance during voltage spikes and enough power to start the fridge.

One distinction Jackery has over its competition is a choice between instant backup UPS and a delayed start. “Your refrigerator’s compressor needs a little time to recover,” Tyrrel explains. “When it stops, refrigerant pressure remains high on one side of the system. Restarting too swiftly makes the motor work harder and briefly draw several times its normal current. Delayed Start gives the compressor a short pause before restarting, helping avoid unnecessary strain when power flickers on and off.”.

From the moment an outage occurs, Backup Core automatically powers a refrigerator for 15 to 30 hours. At 29 inches long, it’s 5 to 6 inches longer than all of the other units, but rotating it can fit one atop even a fridge and its slim design should still slip behind the appliance on its vertical wall mount.

Given its size and expansion capabilities, it should come as no surprise that Backup Core also includes the most outlets for electronics. Whereas another model includes one or two ports on the unit, the forward-thinking BioLite design provides its own power strip—that’s three more openings for small kitchen appliances or other electronics to easily connect.

BioLite’s Backup Core is a 1.5 kWh solution, similar to its sister brand Goal Zero Yeti 1500 (6th generation). “However, Backup can expand in 1.5kWh increments with the ‘Extend’ model, and chain up to 10.5kWh of localized capacity,” Rosen explains. That’s even more than the combined 8kWh capacity of the Yeti Pro 4000 and Yeti Pro Tank 4000. So while Backup Core is the priciest of the three, it’s also the only one that can grow into something close to a whole-home battery. Think of it less as a fridge backup and more as the first piece of a backup system.

So we’re celebrating all the things that make old homes worth loving, living in, and fixing up. Learn about historic house styles; find practical advice for maintaining your old home; and discover quirky, forgotten features you simply won’t find in new builds.

  • This chapter goes over the major US emergency powers, including the National Emergencies Act, the Insurrection Act, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), and others, and offers proposals for curbing the dangers they create.

My forthcoming chapter on "Emergency Powers" is now available on SSRN. It is coauthored with Josh Braver (University of Wisconsin), and will be published in the forthcoming Cato Handbook on Executive Power, edited by Molly Nixon. Braver is a leading expert on the law of domestic use of the military and a liberal/progressive. I am a a libertarian. If we can come to agreement on these complications, I hope others can, as well. Here is the abstract:.

Emergency powers are special types of government authorities that are only supposed to be used under extraordinary circumstances, in order to address a crisis. But, over time, many have become institutionalized as near-blank checks that the executive can invoke at will. This situation imperils civil liberties and our constitutional system.

This chapter goes over the major US emergency powers, including the National Emergencies Act, the Insurrection Act, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), and others, and offers proposals for curbing the dangers they create. Effective reform requires a combination of new legislation and strong, nondeferential judicial review.

According to recent reports, I recently covered related concerns in an article for Just Security, which goes over potential legislative reforms. In the Cato Handbook chapter, Braver and I cover both legislative reforms and how judicial review can be strengthened.

For outdoor sports enthusiasts, they keep hands dry and protect against frostbite. For those who work outdoors, they are essential because they offer protection from grease, mud, and other wet messes.

According to recent reports, we searched out a diverse collection of waterproof gloves for a wide variety of tasks in all seasons. Then we tested their ability to keep hands dry and comfortable in tough conditions. The Carhartt Waterproof Insulated Gloves earned our pick as the best waterproof gloves for men for their reliable waterproofing, comfortable insulation, and affordable price, and the MCTi Ski Gloves for Women topped our women’s picks for their watertight protection, flexible fit, and responsive touch-screen fingertips.

Bottom line: Discover the best waterproof gloves of 2026, tested for durability, comfort, and specific needs, ensuring dry and warm hands in any condition.

Sources indicate that we initially selected the following gloves based on the quality of their construction, their durability, and the other features outlined previously. Then we tested them to discover how they held up under wet, slippery conditions. Find out how they performed in the reviews ahead.

Men looking for a long-lasting pair of gloves to keep their hands dry and warm may find what they’re looking for in Carhartt’s waterproof insulated gloves. From the shell to the liner to the palm pad, these gloves are made of 100 percent polyester. They provide a warm, durable, and waterproof barrier between the skin and the elements.

Sources indicate that A liner made with Carhartt’s FastDry moisture-wicking technology prevents sweat from collecting inside the gloves, and a waterproof insert provides an extra layer of protection from the elements. Adjustable hook-and-loop closures and elastic cuffs keep hands snug while keeping out cold air and elements.

Recent findings suggest that in our tests, these Carhartt waterproof work gloves were as comfortable as they were waterproof. They performed perfectly on all three of our waterproof tests. They stayed dry under the shower and when immersed in water while providing excellent holding ability thanks to the textured grip area. Three-dimensional construction lets the hand rest in a natural position and delivers good dexterity for gripping and holding. Although we didn’t test specifically for winter warmth, these gloves are deeply insulated for cold-weather work. However, the bulky profile takes away the ability to pick up small or thin items from a flat surface or to reach into a pants pocket.

What our tester notes: “These got ‘Best Overall’ because they’re not only toasty and affordable, but they also make an excellent choice for winter chores while not looking like work gloves.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer.

On the gloves’ interior, a waterproof liner helps keep moisture from reaching the skin.

According to recent reports, MCTi’s gloves also contain 120 grams of Thinsulate insulation that keeps hands warm in temperatures as cold as -10 degrees Fahrenheit without adding much bulk. Handy elastic wrist leashes make keeping track of the gloves easier if the wearer removes them, and sensitive touch-screen pads on three fingers allow the wearer to answer a phone or send a text without having to take off the gloves.

In our tests, these ski gloves by MCTi seemed more like general-use winter gloves. The waterproof feature is on point, with zero water intrusion during testing and a capable grip in wet conditions. The touch-screen fingertips worked well. Moreover, they’re available in an assortment of accent colors: gray, red, white, rose, and yellow.

This pair is a good choice for cycling, running, walking, or other outdoor pursuits.

These gloves may not be well suited to subzero temperatures, but they’re suitable for regular winter wear and have some nice features. The gloves’ thumbs and index fingers contain sensors that are touch-screen compatible, and the palms are covered in grippy silica gel pods to help users maintain a good grip on phones and other belongings. Elastic cuffs keep out the elements. These gloves fit snugly; the manufacturer suggests sizing up for a more relaxed fit.

These mid-weight lifestyle gloves are built for everyday travel and tasks in frosty weather, but not in pouring rain. Our rain simulation and immersion tests revealed numerous water entry points. Water resistance was good in our aggressive rain simulation for about a minute before leaks developed, so we believe the gloves could keep hands mostly or completely dry during an average rainstorm. They provided excellent grip for wet items. The touch-screen feature worked well, and the snug, low-profile fit allowed us to pick up a key that was lying flat on a countertop. Youngstown Glove Tech giant’s FR Waterproof Leather Utility gloves incorporate both leather and Kevlar, a synthetic fabric commonly used for protection, along with a waterproof, windproof, breathable polyurethane barrier. These gloves, which have earned American National Standards Institute (ANSI) compliance for welding, provide Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)-approved protection for a wide range of tasks. However, they don’t provide adequate protection for electrical work.

Youngstown’s waterproof utility work gloves delivered good waterproof and wet-grip performances in our three wet tests. Although we got the leather so thoroughly wet that the gloves became heavy, the waterproof barrier prevented water intrusion to the skin. Wet grip was not a problem. We were pleasantly surprised by the dexterity that these bulky gloves provided, thanks to their three-dimensional construction and a naturally relaxed hand posture. Overall, we would not recommend these gloves for extended use in a watery environment because those conditions would cause the leather to degrade promptly. However, those who need a sturdy and comfortable insulated glove for working in the elements may want to look at these.

Carhartt’s Cold Snap insulated work gloves offer both cold-weather protection and long-lasting construction that’s tough enough for the jobsite. With warm insulation on the outer shell and a reinforced palm, these polyester gloves are reinforced with leather for extra durability. They’re waterproof and have a nose wipe on the thumb, making them a good choice for working in rough weather.

Cold Snap gloves feature some of Carhartt’s proprietary materials, including a FastDry lining for wicking moisture and Storm Defender waterproofing treatment. They have a thick cuff with an adjustable drawstring for improved weather protection. A small section of goatskin around the finger and thumb area provides added grip.

Recent findings suggest that our second pair of Carhartt waterproof work gloves performed nearly as well as the first. It provided excellent waterproof and wet-grip performance along with excellent dexterity, considering the lofty insulation. The polyester and leather exterior sheds water very well instead of becoming saturated and heavy. We liked the drawcord cuff on these gloves a little less than we liked the hook-and-loop strap closure on our “Best Overall” selection because the barrel-cord tightener is harder to manipulate with gloved hands. Nevertheless, pairing outstanding waterproofing, warmth, and comfort with a great look is the winning recipe for an all-around great pair of gloves.

Get the Carhartt Cold Snap waterproof gloves on Amazon.

It has been revealed that no more freezing hands when you try to take a pic or return an notable text. These low-profile knitted Sealskinz gloves offer triple-layer insulated waterproof, windproof protection from the elements with touch-screen-capable fingertips and outstanding range of motion. The nylon and elastane outer layer offers excellent durability with silicone-printed grips on the palm and fingers for a secure grip. A mid-layer windproof, waterproof, breathable membrane keeps the warmth in and the elements out. The lining is made of merino wool, nylon, and elastane for added warmth and breathability.

These Sealskinz gloves offered a lot of things we really liked but a few things we didn’t. They also offer outstanding wet-grip capability, with touch-perfect touch-screen functionality. The low-profile design, moderate amount of insulation, and superior wet performance are perfect for getting outside on those miserable raw days when it’s 30 degrees Fahrenheit with freezing rain. But we didn’t love the semi-absorbent exterior because it holds on to more than its share of water, even though the water never reached our hands. It makes these otherwise excellent gloves feel heavy and a little bit squelchy. However, these may be the best gloves when wet weather threatens.

Get the Sealskinz waterproof gloves at Amazon or Sealskinz.

Hestra’s Army Leather Heli Ski 3-Finger Gloves are designed for men and women who spend their time atop some of the coldest mountains. These three-finger gloves are constructed from Hestra’s windproof, breathable, and water-resistant Triton fabric, with goat leather on the palms and fingers for improved grip in cold and slippery conditions.

The insides of these Hestra gloves are made of a very thin polyester fiber with efficient insulating properties, which makes them warm without being overly bulky. The oversize cuffs feature a drawstring closure to keep out snow and moisture, and leashes ensure the gloves won’t get lost. These Army Leather Heli gloves are available in three colors.

Recent findings suggest that these gloves looked great and performed better than expected in our tests, but they were not totally waterproof. We anticipated soaking-wet hands because of the leather and “water- resistant” fabric. In our tests, the leather eventually became wet, and some moisture from outside did seep inside. They offered an OK but not great grip when wet. The best advantages of these gloves are the finger configuration, which offers better warmth than a conventional glove and better articulation than a mitten. That stated, we did not test for performance in cold weather. On the downside, the leather must be regularly oiled (a tube is included), and they take a long time to dry once wet.

Get the Hestra Heli waterproof gloves at Amazon, REI, or Backcountry.com.

According to recent reports, built in the style of traditional cuff-length work gloves, Hestra Job Titan Flex Gloves bring the outstanding comfort and durability of goatskin leather with waterproof neoprene cuffs and Hestra Flex fabric. The stress points on the palm and fingers are reinforced with double-layered leather, while the index fingers and thumbs feature touch-screen pads for convenience. These three-season work gloves are lined with moisture-wicking fleece for added warmth and comfort in cold, wet weather.

In a recent development, in our tests, these gloves provided good waterproof protection and excellent wet-gripping ability. They resisted water penetration for over a minute before moisture found its entry point at the edges of the touch-screen pad on the index finger. The touch-screen pad functioned well, and the glove offered good dexterity and comfort overall, but the sizing runs a bit small. The moderate price point and durable construction make them ideal spring, fall, or mild winter weather general-use work gloves.

We selected and tested a diverse assortment of waterproof gloves designed for a variety of uses in different seasons. For all of them, our key testing consideration was whether the gloves were truly waterproof. To find out, we used three testing methods and allowed the gloves to thoroughly dry between tests. All comments about sizing are subjective, based on sizing guides provided by the manufacturers and perceived comfort by the tester. On those gloves not listed as unisex, women tested women’s gloves, and men tested men’s gloves.

According to recent reports, first, we simulated storm conditions with a rain-wand attachment on a garden hose. The testers wore each pair of gloves beneath a steady 2-minute shower, flexing their hands and turning them over to expose all parts of the gloves to the stream. In the second test, we immersed our gloved hands into a bucket of water, again flexing and rotating to ensure that they were completely wet. Finally, we tested them for wet-gripping ability while handling smooth wet stones. To merit inclusion in this guide, each pair of gloves passed all three tests with minimal water intrusion to the inside of the glove.

Sources indicate that before shopping for the best waterproof gloves, consider the type of work planned for the gloves as well as the kind of materials and construction desired. In this section, we review some key considerations to keep in mind while shopping for the best waterproof gloves, including materials, use, fit, and more.

According to recent reports, choosing the best waterproof gloves depends on how they’ll be used. Work gloves are completely different from those intended for outdoor sports or casual wear.

It has been revealed that on garments labeled “waterproof,” the outer shell is usually where the magic happens. Materials like tightly woven nylon, polyester, softshell technical materials, treated leather, and others work well to shed water before it can seep through to the lining. Keep in mind that it’s very rare for leather gloves to actually be waterproof; more likely, they are simply water-resistant.

Aside from shell material, other elements in waterproof gloves’ exteriors make them useful in wet or messy situations. Some of the best waterproof gloves, for example, have textured grips that make it easier for the wearer to grab on to wet, slippery surfaces, making them ideal for skiing, cycling, and other active pursuits. Those looking for waterproof gloves for work may want to invest in gloves with reinforced palms and thumbs, which should last longer and stand up to more wear.

The best waterproof gloves contain an optional outer shell with conductors that transfer the electrical charge from a finger to a touch screen, allowing users to manipulate their phones without removing their gloves.

In a recent development, some of the best waterproof gloves contain insulation that captures body heat, which forms air pockets that warm with the heat from the hand. Most insulation is a man-made poly-fill material such as Thinsulate or 3M.

Sources indicate that to ensure gloves keep warm air inside and cold air from seeping in, some waterproof gloves have long elastic cuffs that hug tight to the wrist and arm, closing off any pathway for air to enter. For even warmer gloves, look for removable liners that can slip inside a waterproof glove to add another layer of insulation.

It has been revealed that when selecting the best waterproof gloves, fit and comfort are essential. However, a “good fit” is relative to the activity. A pair of running gloves fits quite differently than a pair of winter work gloves or ski gloves.

Sources indicate that waterproof running or hiking gloves often feel like a stretchy, flexible second skin. Because they’re lightweight and wick away moisture, users sometimes forget they’re even wearing them.

According to recent reports, waterproof work gloves are bulkier and a bit stiff because they’re generally made from thick nylon or leather that resists ripping, tearing, and friction. Moreover, extra padding or reinforcement on the thumbs or palms can add to their bulk. Though work gloves fit loosely, they shouldn’t be so loose that it’s difficult to pick up small items while wearing them.

According to recent reports, ski gloves are flexible but don’t wear particularly well because they’re typically made from materials like nylon. Properly fitting ski gloves fit snugly around the wrist but are roomy enough to allow the skier to manipulate straps on ski poles and boot bindings.

Also consider breathability. If hands sweat and moisture collects inside the glove, it won’t matter that the shell is waterproof because hands will still get wet. Breathable gloves help some of the heat and moisture escape without letting in cold outer air and moisture.

Now that you know a bit more about the factors to consider when choosing the best waterproof gloves for your needs, some questions may remain. The following are some of the most frequently asked questions about the best waterproof gloves, so check for an answer to your question below.

Waterproof means that absolutely no water makes its way into the glove. Water-resistant means that the gloves shed water to a degree before water comes in.

As one of the best options for the warmest waterproof gloves, the Carhartt Cold Snap waterproof gloves are warm enough to protect your hands in very cold temperatures.

You can wash some waterproof gloves, but it’s best to spot clean them and use a boot dryer with a glove attachment if they become soiled.

The best way to dry the inside of waterproof gloves is to put them on a boot dryer with a glove attachment.
